4 min read
Just now

--

feels productive to code like thisFirst off, I have zero scientific evidence for this. Like, actually none. If you’re looking for a peer-reviewed study or something, you’re in the wrong place. This is basically just based on a few things I’ve noticed, way too much caffeine, a weird amount of anime, and the random confidence you get after watching one productivity video at 2 AM.
Now that we’ve established I’m completely unqualified, let’s get into it.
Every time I go on GitHub, I see devs arguing about which framework is “the one.” Is it React? Vue? Angular? Svelte? Or some random framework that came out ten minutes ago by some guy named Evan in a coffee shop?
Meanwhile, somewhere in Japan — at least in the version of Japan that exists in productivity videos — a student just opens a textbook and starts solving problems without tweeting:
Day 14 of my coding journey. Today I optimized my productivity stack.
Coincidence?
Probably. But let me pretend it isn’t.
The average dev’s learning process usually goes like this:
“I want to learn JavaScript.”
Three hours later…
“Actually, I should probably learn TypeScript.”
Twenty minutes later…
“Wait, companies use Next.js.”
Forty-five minutes later…
“Maybe AI engineering is the future.”
The next morning…
“I heard cybersecurity pays way more.”
By lunch…
“I should just become a farmer.”
Somehow we manage to change careers five times before even writing our first function.
The imaginary Japanese student doesn’t do any of that. They open the book. They study. They close the book. Imagine that.
No Notion template. No “second brain.” No Obsidian vault with 14,000 notes called The Philosophy of Arrays. Just… studying.
Meanwhile, devs spend four hours picking the perfect VS Code theme before finally writing:
console.log("Hello World")Peak productivity.
Also, devs have a weird relationship with tutorials. We don’t actually watch them; we collect them. My browser usually looks like this:

• Complete React Course

• React in 30 Minutes

• React Is Dead

• Why React Will Never Die

• Should You Learn React in 2026?

• Why I Regret Learning React
At this point, I know everything about React except how to actually use React.
Then the imaginary Japanese student walks in. One textbook. One pen. One chair. They leave three hours later knowing more than I learned from six playlists and fourteen open tabs. It’s honestly rude.
Planning is another hobby devs mistake for actually making progress.
Monday: “I’m making a roadmap.”
Tuesday: “Improving the roadmap.”
Wednesday: “Redesigning the roadmap.”
Thursday: “Found a better roadmap.”
Friday: “Bought a roadmap course.”
Saturday: “I should probably start learning now.”
Sunday: “I deserve a break.”
Productivity level: Legendary.
We also love optimizing everything except the thing that actually matters.
Mechanical keyboard? Optimized.
Monitor arm? Optimized.
Standing desk? Optimized.
RGB lights? Optimized.
Coffee setup? Optimized.
Desk plant? Optimized.
Learning? Scheduled for next Monday.
Then we make up fancy names for simple things.
“I studied for two hours” is boring. But “I conducted a Deep Cognitive Neural Knowledge Acquisition Session” makes me sound like some Silicon Valley founder raising $12 million. Nothing actually changed, though. I still spent thirty minutes picking the “perfect” Spotify playlist to maximize my brain waves.
Speaking of playlists… devs really believe there’s one magical playlist that unlocks hidden intelligence. Lo-fi, classical, rain sounds, rain sounds in a spaceship, rain sounds in a Japanese café, rain sounds recorded on Mars. None of them helped because I spent twenty minutes reading the YouTube comments anyway.
Then there’s the setup. Dual monitors. Triple monitors. Ultrawide. Vertical. One monitor has the docs, one has Stack Overflow, one has YouTube, and one has a cat livestream. And somehow the only monitor not showing code is the actual code editor. Engineering at its finest.
Then there’s the perfectionism. Devs don’t write bad code; we just delay writing any code until we’re “capable” of writing perfect code. Which basically means writing nothing. Great strategy. Would procrastinate again.
The imaginary Japanese student doesn’t care. The first solution is ugly. The second one is less ugly. The tenth one finally works. Meanwhile, I’m spending forty-five minutes deciding if userDataFinalFinal2 is a good variable name. (It isn't).
And the productivity apps. Every month there’s a new app that promises to change your life. One uses AI, one uses neuroscience, one uses blockchain for no reason, one gamifies your habits. Congrats, you now have seven different apps reminding you that you’re not being productive.
Eventually, something funny happens. The student who quietly studies every day actually gets skilled. The dev who watches 300 productivity videos becomes an expert on… productivity videos.
Turns out learning isn’t about finding the “perfect system.” It’s just about doing something hard over and over until it becomes easier. A really disappointing answer. I was hoping the solution was just buying another keyboard.
So, do Japanese students actually learn faster? Probably not. But the version of them we’ve made up — the one who just sits down and focuses — reminds us of something we try to ignore:

• Consistency beats excitement.

• Finishing beats preparing.

• One finished book beats a hundred bookmarked books.

• A thousand lines of terrible code beat a thousand videos about writing perfect code.
So close YouTube. Close Reddit. Close the forty tabs explaining how to learn. Open your editor. Write some terrible code. Tomorrow, write slightly less terrible code.
Keep doing that, and one day someone on LinkedIn will call you an “experienced software engineer.” Which is basically how it happens in real life.
